source_note: Content based on the compiled reference note “Global AI Governance Framework — Civilian and Military Dimensions”, September 2026. It is a working reference: verify primary UN document numbers and other details before citing in official correspondence.

paragraphs: “Global AI governance framework” is not a single instrument. It is a layered patchwork of political principles, binding treaties, national statutes, technical standards, and multilateral processes that different bodies have built to manage AI risks and benefits across borders. As of 2026, the international coordination landscape is best described as a “weak regime complex”: multiple coordination points exist — the UN Advisory Body on AI, the Hiroshima AI Process (G7), the Council of Europe AI Convention, and the Bletchley Declaration — but no single binding global rulebook covers AI comprehensively.

Governance is increasingly shaped by geopolitical competition rather than pure technical coordination: the US AI Action Plan, China's Global AI Governance Action Plan, and the EU AI Act's extraterritorial reach all reflect states using AI governance as an instrument of strategic positioning, raising risks of regulatory arbitrage and normative fragmentation.

paragraphs: This track explicitly excludes civilian AI by its own text and addresses the full lifecycle of military AI — pre-design, design, development, evaluation, testing, deployment, use, sale, procurement, operation and decommissioning — rather than autonomous weapons alone.

blocks.text: A recurring critique in the literature is that industry self-governance mixes safety commitments with commercial competition among the same companies, producing inconsistent compliance. One tracking effort measured a mean compliance rate of roughly 53% across 30 safety indicators among major labs, ranging from about 13% to 83% depending on the company — a useful data point when industry self-regulation comes up in multilateral consultations.

sections.title: National and regional AI regulatory approaches
sections.intro: Countries and regions take significantly different regulatory approaches to AI, ranging from strict horizontal legislation and targeted state oversight to light-touch, innovation-first strategies.

items: Civilian AI governance is anchored by voluntary norm-setters (OECD, UNESCO) with the EU AI Act and the CoE Framework Convention as the only binding instruments to date; the UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance is the newest and least-formed multilateral track.

Military AI governance runs on two parallel and increasingly divergent tracks: the CCW/GGE process on LAWS specifically (tight-regulation coalition) and the REAIM/Political Declaration process on the broader military AI domain (responsible-use coalition).

The three consecutive UNGA LAWS resolutions (2023–2025) show a pattern of narrowing procedural mandates even as vote counts remain high — the 2025 text only “encouraged” further exchanges rather than mandating new consultations, and the US shifted from abstention to voting against.

Austria and Pakistan are both co-sponsors of the broader “AI in the military domain” resolution track (A/RES/79/239 and its 2025 follow-up), which is distinct from the narrower LAWS-specific resolution track.

The HLAB-AI's “Governing AI for Humanity” report remains the most comprehensive UN diagnostic of governance gaps, highlighting that 118 mostly Global South states are excluded from major AI governance initiatives.

Industry self-governance (FMF, safety frameworks, HAIP) fills operational gaps left by slower-moving multilateral processes, but faces credibility questions due to uneven compliance and inherent conflicts of interest.
